title: The Heap, and Why Every Manual Delete Is Eventually Wrong

questions.question: What is the difference between the stack and the heap?
options: Stack objects are destroyed automatically when their scope ends, heap objects must be given back explicitly
The stack is faster but holds only numbers
The heap is destroyed automatically, the stack is not
There is no difference, they are two names for the same memory
questions.explanation: The stack unwinds automatically as functions return. The heap serves objects whose size is unknown until runtime or that must outlive their creator, and it requires an explicit release.

questions.question: Why is a manual delete at the bottom of a function fragile?
options: The cleanup is attached to a place in the text, so every new way out must remember it
Because delete is slow
Because the compiler may reorder it
Because delete can only be called once per program
questions.explanation: Leaks arrive when somebody adds an early return or a throw and never looks at the bottom of the function. The problem is structural rather than carelessness.

questions.question: What must new[] be paired with?
options: delete[]
delete
free
Either delete or delete[], they are equivalent
questions.explanation: The bracket forms must match. Mixing them is undefined behaviour and frequently does not crash immediately, which makes it harder to find than if it did.

questions.question: In the reference, why was the early return turned into a break?
options: It leaves the loop but not the function, so there is still exactly one place that gives the memory back
Because return is not allowed inside a loop
Because break is faster than return
To avoid copying the return value
questions.explanation: One way out means one delete. It is the cheapest possible fix and it survives somebody adding a third exit condition later.

questions.question: How do the tests prove nothing leaked, without any tooling?
options: They count allocations and frees by replacing operator new and operator delete
They measure how much memory the process is using
They run each test twice and compare the timing
They rely on the compiler warning about it
questions.explanation: Counting is deterministic and identical on every platform. Arrays and single objects are counted separately, so a mismatched new and delete pair is caught too.

questions.question: How much bare new and delete should appear in production C++?
options: Almost none: std::vector when the size varies, and an owning smart pointer when an object must outlive its creator
As much as necessary, since it is the only way to use the heap
Only inside classes
Only in code that talks to hardware
questions.explanation: Both give the memory back on every path automatically. That is the conclusion of the argument in this lesson rather than a rule handed down.
